title: Borrowed phrases
note: Serious prose borrows freely from Latin (sine qua non, without which not; quid pro quo, something for something), French (bête noire, black beast; fait accompli, accomplished fact) and German (Zeitgeist, time-spirit). English usually keeps the French accents (bête, célèbre, grâce) and often capitalizes the German nouns, as German does.

items.a: an essential condition; something indispensable
d: a thing already done and unchangeable
items.ex: For a field hospital, clean water is the sine qua non.

items.a: a person or thing one especially dislikes or dreads
d: a person who shocks the establishment
items.ex: Split infinitives were the old editor's bête noire.

items.a: required by custom, fashion, or etiquette
d: unique; in a class of its own
items.ex: Black tie was de rigueur at the gala.

items.a: the chief reason for something's existence
items.ex: Saving the old theater was the society's raison d'être.

items.a: a thing already done, so no longer open to dispute
d: a plan drawn up for one purpose
items.ex: By the time the board met, the sale was a fait accompli.

items.a: formed or done for a particular purpose only
d: in the middle of the action
items.ex: An ad hoc committee was formed to plan the reunion.

items.a: to a tiresome, sickening extent
items.ex: He told the fishing story ad nauseam.

items.a: something given in return for something else
items.ex: The endorsement looked like a quid pro quo for the contract.

items.a: an acknowledgment of one's own fault
items.ex: The CEO's mea culpa came only after the recall.

items.a: complete freedom to act as one wishes
items.ex: The new chef was given carte blanche to redesign the menu.

items.a: a controversial issue or case that draws wide attention
items.ex: The wrongful arrest became a cause célèbre.

items.a: a final blow that ends something
items.ex: The third failed inspection was the coup de grâce for the restaurant.

items.a: a phrase with two meanings, one often risqué
d: a remark made in an aside
items.ex: The comedian's act depended on double entendres.

items.a: a person whose unconventional brilliance shocks the establishment
items.ex: The architect was the enfant terrible of the profession.

items.a: shared pride and loyalty among a group's members
items.ex: Night drills built esprit de corps among the recruits.

items.a: a pleasing quality that is hard to describe
items.ex: The old café had a certain je ne sais quoi.

items.a: a policy of leaving things to take their own course
d: a policy of regaining lost land
items.ex: The coach's laissez-faire style let players run their own drills.

items.a: a characteristic way of working
items.ex: The burglar's modus operandi was to enter through the dog door.

items.a: an unwelcome or unacceptable person
items.ex: After the expulsion, the diplomat was declared persona non grata.

items.a: done as a formality
items.ex: The vote was pro forma; the deal was already signed.

items.a: unknown territory or an unexplored subject
items.ex: For most voters, the tax code is terra incognita.

items.a: a performance or achievement of great skill
items.ex: Her final-round chess game was a tour de force.

items.a: the defining spirit or mood of a period
d: a ghost said to haunt a house
items.ex: The film captured the anxious Zeitgeist of the 1970s.

items.a: a comprehensive view of the world and life
d: the mood of a particular decade
items.ex: The novelist's Weltanschauung was bleak but never cynical.

items.a: into the middle of a narrative or action
d: at the very end of a story
items.ex: The "Iliad" opens in medias res, years into the war.

items.a: unique; in a class by itself
items.ex: Part bookstore, part bar, the place was sui generis.

items.a: a passionate appeal or protest
d: a battle cry before an attack
items.ex: Her letter to the council was a cri de coeur for the closing library.

items.a: at first sight; accepted as correct until disproved
items.ex: The receipts were prima facie evidence of the payments.

items.a: the voice of the people; popular opinion
items.ex: Talk radio claimed to speak for the vox populi.

items.a: an improbable device that suddenly resolves a plot
items.ex: A rich uncle arriving in the final scene is a classic deus ex machina.

read.title: A Restaurant in Three Acts
text: When Ana Ruiz took over her family's diner, her mother gave her carte blanche on one condition: the Sunday pancakes stayed. That was the sine qua non. Everything else was terra incognita.

Ana's modus operandi was to change one thing a week. She replaced the paper menus, fixed the flickering sign, and hired a cook who had trained in Lyon. Some regulars treated each change as a fait accompli they had never agreed to, and one wrote angry letters to the local paper ad nauseam. The loudest critic, a retired judge, became her bête noire.

The turning point came in the middle of a Sunday rush, when the grill caught fire. Ana herself put it out, served every table cold cereal with an apology, and printed a mea culpa on the next week's menu. The story spread, and the little diner briefly became a cause célèbre online.
The judge came back the following Sunday. He ordered pancakes, ate them in silence, and left a note: "Prima facie, still good." It was not quite praise, but in that town it was close.

Years later, food writers credited Ana with capturing the Zeitgeist: comfort food done with care. She disagreed. The diner, she said, was not sui generis. It was just a place that kept its promises, which, in her view, was the whole raison d'être of a restaurant.

q.q: What was the one condition attached to Ana's carte blanche?
o: She could not hire new cooks
The Sunday pancakes had to stay
She had to keep the paper menus
She had to close on Sundays

q.q: What did Ana's printed mea culpa express?
o: An apology for the fire and the cold meal
A plan to sell the diner

q.q: The judge's note "Prima facie, still good" means the food
